Damaraland mole-rats (Fukomys damarensis) display a suite of life-history traits that are highly unusual among rodents, with many values measured under controlled captive conditions at a body temperature of 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C]. Neonates emerge from the birth canal weighing just 9 grams [Wwb = 9 grams], an altricial mass that reflects the extremely altricial state of the newborn pups. These altricial neonates are entirely dependent on maternal care during the initial postnatal period, and they remain in the natal burrow system for an extended interval. The suckling juvenile stage persists until weaning, which occurs at approximately 28 days after birth [tx = approximately 28 days after birth] under standard thermal conditions of 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C]. This weaning age is notably prolonged compared to many other African mole-rat species, a delay that likely relates to the challenges of acquiring solid food resources in the arid, subterranean environment. The relatively extended nursing stage ensures that the pre-weaning pup attains sufficient body condition to transition to a diet of underground geophytes and tubers.

Gestation in this eutherian species is another remarkably protracted period for a rodent of its size, lasting 93 days [tg = 93 days] when the gestating embryo develops at a maternal core temperature of 35.3 °C [T = 35.3 °C]. This lengthy gestation, which is almost three times longer than what would be predicted for a mammal of this body mass, encompasses a substantial period of organogenesis and foetal development. The extended embryogenesis period is thought to be a consequence of the species' slow metabolic pace and its cooperative breeding system, where reproductive suppression of subordinate females reduces the selective pressure for rapid offspring production. The placental foetus undergoes considerable growth in utero, and the high degree of altriciality at parturition is offset by the sophisticated social environment of the colony, where non-breeding helpers assist with thermoregulation and provisioning of the newborn offspring. The live birth event itself is a critical phase within the sealed burrow system, requiring precise coordination among colony members.

Sexual maturation, marking the onset of gametogenesis, is a delayed event in Damaraland mole-rats. Puberty is attained at approximately 511 days after birth [tp = approximately 511 days after birth] under the typical thermal regime of 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C], an age that is exceptionally prolonged for a rodent and more reminiscent of the developmental schedules seen in large-bodied ungulates or primates. This temporal delay in reproductive activation is intimately linked to the species' cooperative breeding structure, where only a single breeding female and one or two males within a colony typically reproduce. The other colony members, which are reproductively suppressed, nevertheless reach gonadal maturity at this age but do not initiate reproductive cycling unless they disperse and establish a new burrow system. This delayed puberty serves to minimize within-colony reproductive conflict and allows subordinate individuals to contribute to alloparental care. The pace of sexual maturation is thus a central axis of the species' unique life-history strategy.

The maximum reproductive rate of a breeding female under optimal laboratory conditions is remarkably low, reflecting the species' investment in a few, high-quality offspring. Females produce an average of 12 pups per year [Ri = 12 pups per year], and typically a single litter each year [F_R_i = single litter each year] when maintained at a stable body temperature of 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C]. This extremely low annual reproductive output stands in stark contrast to the high fecundity of most muroid rodents. The constraint is partly explained by the very long gestation period and the extended interval of lactation, which together consume nearly one-third of the annual cycle. Furthermore, the breeding female must compete for colony resources, and her fecundity is mediated by the availability of geophytic food resources in the arid Kalahari environment. This reproductive strategy aligns with a classic slow life-history pace.

Longevity in this species is extraordinarily high for a rodent, with maximum lifespan recorded at 15.2 years [am = 15.2 years] under the thermoneutral conditions of 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C]. This places the Damaraland mole-rat among the longest-lived rodents known, far exceeding predictions based on body mass alone. The ultimate wet weight of a fully grown adult is approximately 100 grams [Wwi = approximately 100 grams], making the species a medium-sized bathyergid. The combination of a small body size with an exceptionally extended lifespan and delayed reproduction points to a life-history strategy shaped by low extrinsic mortality in the stable, predator-buffered subterranean niche. Comparative analyses with other African mole-rats suggest that sociality and cooperative breeding relax the selective pressures for rapid life cycles, allowing for the evolution of extreme longevity. This remarkable lifespan places Fukomys damarensis in a small group of mammalian species where senescence is notably slow and age-related physiological decline is postponed until very late in life.
